```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

Class enumeration refers to the process of determining the number of latent
classes to be retained in an analysis. In latent profile analysis (LPA), these
classes are referred to as *profiles*. The number of profiles is not estimated
directly by the model; rather, it is specified a priori by the analyst. The
model is then fitted to the data under the specified number of profiles,
yielding a solution containing exactly that number. Class enumeration
therefore involves fitting a sequence of models with progressively increasing
numbers of profiles, typically beginning with a one-profile model, and
evaluating their relative adequacy to determine which solution best
represents the underlying structure of the data.

The selection of the number of profiles is consequential because it
determines the structure and interpretation of the entire subsequent
analysis. A model with too few profiles may combine substantively distinct
groups of observations into a single profile, resulting in estimated means
that adequately characterize none of the underlying groups. Conversely, a
model with too many profiles may divide a genuine profile into smaller, less
distinct groups that reflect sampling variability rather than meaningful
heterogeneity. Additional profiles may also capture features of the
measurement structure, such as residual correlations among indicators, rather
than substantively distinct patterns of observations. Consequently, the
number of profiles affects their estimated means, relative proportions, the
assignment of observations to profiles, and the conclusions of subsequent
analyses based on profile membership. In the data examined in this article,
the two-profile and four-profile solutions provide different representations
of the same enrolments. However, only one of these solutions corresponds to
the data-generating structure, illustrating that a model with more profiles
does not necessarily provide a more accurate representation of the
underlying population.

In a two-level latent profile analysis, class enumeration concerns three
distinct specifications, each of which must be determined by the analyst:

- **The number of profiles.** Profiles represent distinct patterns of
  observations at the lower level, in this article course enrolments, and are
  defined by their means on the indicators.
- **The number of group classes.** Group classes represent distinct types of
  groups at the upper level, in this article students, and are defined by the
  probability with which the observations of their groups belong to each
  profile. Because group classes are defined in terms of the profiles, a
  model with a single profile cannot contain more than one group class.
- **The covariance structure.** The covariance structure determines whether
  the indicators are allowed to be correlated within a profile and whether
  profiles may differ in the size, shape and orientation of their
  distributions (`EEI`, `VVI`, `EEE` and `VVV`; Celeux & Govaert, 1995).

Class enumeration involves fitting and comparing models across alternative
specifications of the number of profiles, the number of group classes, and
the model structures under consideration. The objective is to identify the
model that provides the most adequate representation of the data while
accounting for model complexity and the substantive characteristics of the
resulting profiles and group classes.

Conventional likelihood ratio tests are generally not appropriate for
comparing finite mixture models that differ in the number of profiles or
group classes. In such comparisons, the model with fewer classes can be
viewed as a constrained version of the more complex model in which the
probability of an additional class is fixed at zero. This restriction places
the parameter on the boundary of the parameter space, violating the
regularity conditions required for the usual chi-squared approximation of
the likelihood ratio statistic (McLachlan, 1987). Alternative procedures
include the parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test (McLachlan, 1987) and
the Lo-Mendell-Rubin approximate likelihood ratio test (Lo et al., 2001),
available for supported models through `bootstrap_lrt()` and
`get_results(x, "lmr")`, respectively. These
tests require repeated model estimation and, consequently, careful
evaluation of convergence and estimation stability.

Information criteria provide a complementary approach to model comparison by
balancing model fit, typically represented by the log likelihood, against a
penalty for model complexity. The Akaike information criterion (AIC; Akaike,
1974), Bayesian information criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978), sample-size
adjusted BIC (Sclove, 1987), consistent AIC (CAIC; Bozdogan, 1987), and
Kullback information criterion (KIC; Cavanaugh, 1999) incorporate penalties
related to the number of estimated parameters. In contrast, the integrated
classification likelihood (ICL; Biernacki et al., 2000), approximate weight
of evidence (AWE; Banfield & Raftery, 1993), and classification likelihood
criterion (CLC; Biernacki & Govaert, 1997) additionally account for
classification uncertainty. These criteria therefore tend to favour
solutions in which profiles and group classes are more clearly separated and
observations can be assigned with greater certainty.

The various enumeration procedures do not necessarily identify the same
model, and their relative performance depends on the characteristics of the
model and the data. A simulation study by
[Nylund, Asparouhov, and Muthén (2007)](https://www.statmodel.com/bmuthen/articles/Article_111.pdf)
found that the BIC and the bootstrap likelihood ratio test performed
particularly well among the methods examined. Subsequent simulation research
indicated that the AIC and relative entropy perform poorly in identifying
the number of classes and that no criterion achieves adequate power when
classes are weakly separated (Tein et al., 2013). Moreover, implementation of
the Lo-Mendell-Rubin test differs between Mplus and Latent GOLD (Vermunt,
2024), highlighting the importance of considering software-specific
procedures when interpreting test results.

Current recommendations therefore emphasize evaluating a range of candidate
models, reporting the available fit indices and statistical tests, and
integrating these results with classification diagnostics and substantive
interpretability (Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018; Spurk et al., 2020; Weller et
al., 2020; Sorgente et al., 2025). Entropy should be interpreted as a measure
of classification quality for a given model rather than as a standalone
criterion for determining the number of classes. The final selection should
reflect the collective evidence from model fit, classification uncertainty,
estimation stability, and the substantive meaningfulness of the resulting
profiles and group classes. Houle et al. (2026) provide corresponding
guidance for class enumeration in multilevel latent profile analysis.

These three specifications are not independent of one another and should
therefore be evaluated jointly rather than sequentially. A diagonal
covariance structure assumes that the indicators are uncorrelated within each
profile. When this assumption is violated, the model can represent the
residual association among the indicators only by introducing additional
profiles, and the enumeration consequently overstates the number of profiles.
In a similar manner, dependence among the observations of a group that the
model does not represent, such as change across a sequence of courses, may be
absorbed by additional group classes. A criterion that continues to decrease
throughout the candidate range may reflect such departures from the model
rather than a substantively meaningful set of profiles. For the number of
group classes, the sample-size convention of the BIC is also consequential:
the package reports criteria based on both the number of groups and the
number of observations, and Lukočienė et al. (2010) recommend basing the
choice of the number of group classes on the number of groups.

This vignette uses `enumerate_classes()` to fit a grid of two-level latent
profile models over numbers of profiles, numbers of group classes and
covariance structures. It examines information criteria, changes between
adjacent candidates, descriptive curve summaries, classification diagnostics,
and estimation diagnostics. Selected models are compared and a fitted
candidate is extracted for further analysis. No single statistic is treated
as a conclusive estimate of the number of classes.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_enrolments <- nrow(course_engagement)
n_students <- with(course_engagement, length(unique(student)))
```

## Data

The examples use `course_engagement`, a simulated data frame in long format
with one row per course enrolment. It contains
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments of `r n_students`
students. Five measures of activity in each course serve as indicators:
browsing of the course site, lecture viewing, reading of the forum, posting
to the forum and attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course,
so a value of zero is the course average. The column `student` identifies the
student to whom each enrolment belongs. The simulation is calibrated to the
engagement data of students followed through a full study programme (Saqr &
López-Pernas, 2021; Saqr et al., 2023). It was generated from two profiles
and two kinds of students, and `attendance` is generated from the four click
measures, so the indicators are correlated within profiles
(`?course_engagement`).

```{r data}
head(course_engagement)
```

Enrolments are nested in students. The profiles therefore describe patterns
of activity in a single course, and the group classes describe students by
how their enrolments are distributed across those patterns.

## Fitting the candidate models

The candidates are fitted with `enumerate_classes()` from the data, the
indicators in `vars` and the group identifier in `id`. The arguments
`n_profiles` and `n_group_classes` give the numbers of classes to try, and
one model is fitted for every combination of them. Here the numbers of
profiles and of group classes both run from one to four. The argument `model`
sets the covariance structure of the profiles; without it, as here, the four
basic structures `EEI`, `VVI`, `EEE` and `VVV` are fitted for every
combination.

Mixture likelihoods can have multiple local maxima, so each candidate is
estimated from several starting values. The `n_starts` argument controls the
number of fully fitted starts and `seed` controls reproducibility. This
example uses five starts per candidate to limit computation. An applied
analysis should assess whether increasing the number of starts changes the
selected likelihood or substantive conclusions.

Every estimation argument, such as `n_starts`, applies identically to all
candidates, and a grid is re-estimated in its entirety when more starts are
required, so that every candidate has the same opportunity to reach its
maximum. When many starts are used, a candidate with more profiles than the
data support can reach a degenerate solution in which one profile collapses
on a single observation with every variance at its lower bound; its
likelihood, and hence its criteria, then depend on `min_variance` rather than
on the data. A profile can also be spurious without reaching the bound, when
a few nearly coincident observations give it variances close to zero
(McLachlan & Peel, 2000, section 3.10).

A Gaussian component can concentrate around very few observations and
approach a variance bound. The `boundary = "exclude"` option excludes starts
with variances at the configured bound; it does not detect every narrowly
concentrated component. The `latents_thin_profiles` warning flags limited
posterior support relative to the number of profile-specific Gaussian
parameters. This is a diagnostic heuristic rather than an identification
test. Inspect component sizes and covariance diagnostics before interpreting
such a profile.

The default search depends on the covariance specification. EII, EEI and EEE
models use emEM screening: five times `n_starts` starts are screened by a
short EM run each, and the first start and the best of the others, `n_starts` in all, are
continued to convergence
(Biernacki et al., 2003). The other structures start from k-means, because
with profile-specific variances emEM reaches spurious maxima more often. The `search`
argument can override these defaults. The `cores` argument permits parallel
candidate fitting.

```{r enumerate, warning = FALSE}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:4, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
```

```{r models-values, include = FALSE}
candidates <- as.data.frame(models)
n_candidates <- nrow(candidates)
n_failed <- with(candidates, sum(is.na(log_likelihood)))
best <- get_results(models, "best")
pick <- function(name, convention_name) {
  with(subset(best, criterion == name & convention %in% convention_name),
       candidate)
}
bic_groups_pick <- pick("bic", "groups")
bic_individual_pick <- pick("bic", "individuals")
icl_groups_pick <- pick("icl", "groups")
icl_individual_pick <- pick("icl", "individuals")
awe_groups_pick <- pick("awe", "groups")
awe_individual_pick <- pick("awe", "individuals")
aic_pick <- with(subset(best, criterion == "aic"), candidate)
chosen_name <- "profiles2_groups2_VVV"
diagonal <- subset(candidates, model == "VVI" & !is.na(bic_groups))
diagonal_pick <- with(subset(diagonal, bic_groups == min(bic_groups)), candidate)
bic_of <- function(name) with(subset(candidates, candidate == name), bic_groups)
diagonal_bic <- round(bic_of(diagonal_pick))
chosen_bic <- round(bic_of(chosen_name))
bic_gap <- round(bic_of(chosen_name) - bic_of(bic_groups_pick))
# The text below names these candidates; stop if the results ever change.
stopifnot(n_candidates == 64, n_failed == 12,
          bic_groups_pick == "profiles2_groups4_VVV",
          bic_individual_pick == "profiles2_groups3_EEE",
          icl_groups_pick == "profiles2_groups3_VVV",
          icl_individual_pick == "profiles2_groups3_EEE",
          awe_groups_pick == "profiles2_groups2_EEE",
          awe_individual_pick == "profiles2_groups2_VVI",
          aic_pick == "profiles4_groups4_VVV",
          diagonal_pick == "profiles4_groups3_VVI",
          chosen_bic < diagonal_bic)
```

The result records `r n_candidates` requested candidates. Each candidate is
named by its numbers of profiles and group classes and its covariance
structure, so that `profiles2_groups4_VVV` has two profiles, four group
classes and a full covariance per profile; the name identifies the candidate
in every function that follows. The `r n_failed` candidates with one profile
and several group classes could not be estimated. Group classes are defined
by differences in the distribution of profiles, and a model with a single
profile has no such differences. These candidates remain in the table with
the error that stopped them.

## The table of candidates

The table of candidates has one row per candidate and is returned by
`as.data.frame()`; printing `models` shows the same table with a summary of
failed and unreplicated candidates. The 16 candidates with the `VVV`
structure:

```{r table}
subset(as.data.frame(models), model == "VVV")
```

The columns fall into groups.

| Columns | Content |
|---|---|
| `candidate`, `n_profiles`, `n_group_classes`, `model` | Identity of the candidate |
| `log_likelihood`, `n_parameters` | Fit and size |
| `aic`, `kic`, `bic_*`, `sabic_*`, `caic_*`, `awe_*`, `icl_*`, `clc_*` | Information criteria |
| `profile_entropy`, `group_entropy` | Relative entropy at each level |
| `avepp_min`, `avepp_max`, `avepp_mean`, `avepp_below` | Average posterior probability of the profiles |
| `group_avepp_min`, `group_avepp_max`, `group_avepp_mean`, `group_avepp_below` | Average posterior probability of the group classes |
| `converged`, `boundary`, `n_best_replicated`, `warnings`, `error` | Checks of the estimation |

## Information criteria

Many information criteria combine deviance (minus twice the maximized log
likelihood) with a penalty for the number of estimated parameters. Some
criteria also penalize classification uncertainty. Lower values are preferred
under the chosen criterion. In a two-level model, several parameter penalties
depend on the sample-size convention. Criteria ending in `_groups` count the
`r n_students` students as the independent units, and criteria ending in
`_individual` count the `r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments.
An analysis uses one of the two conventions throughout.

ICL and AWE include uncertainty about both the students' group classes and
their enrolments' profiles under either convention. Changing the sample-size
convention changes the parameter penalty, not which classification
uncertainty is included.

The candidate at the minimum of each criterion:

```{r best}
get_results(models, "best")
```

Most criteria select two profiles; the AIC, the CLC and the SABIC with
students as the units, whose parameter penalties are weakest or absent,
select four, and the CAIC with students as the units three. They
agree that the indicators are correlated within profiles: all but one select
a structure with covariances (`EEE` or `VVV`). They disagree on the number of
group classes. With students as the units, the BIC is lowest for
`r bic_groups_pick`, the ICL for `r icl_groups_pick` and the AWE for
`r awe_groups_pick`; with enrolments as the units, the BIC is lowest for
`r bic_individual_pick`. The AIC is lowest for `r aic_pick`, the largest
candidate fitted.

The covariance structure matters for the number of profiles. Among the
diagonal `VVI` candidates alone, the BIC with students as the units is lowest
for `r diagonal_pick` (BIC `r format(diagonal_bic, big.mark = ",")`): with
the within-profile correlation of attendance excluded, two further profiles
absorb it. Two profiles with free covariances and two group classes fit
better (BIC `r format(chosen_bic, big.mark = ",")`).

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, one line per number
of group classes, for every structure, with the lowest value of each
criterion ringed.

```{r plot-criteria, fig.height = 5}
plot_enumeration(models)
```

A minimum at the largest candidate leaves uncertainty about models beyond
the fitted range. Consider a wider, scientifically plausible range alongside
alternative measurement and covariance specifications. An interior minimum
is not guaranteed. Any criterion can be plotted by name; `what = "all"`
displays every criterion.

```{r plot-bic}
plot_enumeration(models, what = "bic_groups")
```

The tree summarizes correspondence between profiles across independently
fitted models (Zappia & Oshlack, 2018). Links are weighted by shared
posterior membership mass, computed from products of the models' membership
probabilities, rather than by assuming that profiles form nested partitions.
Each number of group classes and structure has its own tree;
`n_group_classes` and `model` select one, and `plot_tree(models)` returns
them all, one plot each. The guide *Tree plot* compares solutions at one
number of profiles and plots the tree of group classes.

```{r plot-tree, fig.height = 6}
plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1, model = "VVV")
```

## Change with each added class

When a criterion decreases across the whole candidate range, successive
changes help describe how much each additional class improves that
criterion. For every candidate, the table reports the decrease in BIC from
the candidate with one profile fewer and the same number of group classes
and structure, and the decrease from the candidate with one group class
fewer. A positive value means that the added class lowered the criterion.
The argument `using` selects another criterion.

The rows of the `VVV` candidates:

```{r deltas}
subset(get_results(models, "deltas"), model == "VVV")
```

```{r deltas-values, include = FALSE}
deltas <- get_results(models, "deltas")
delta_of <- function(name, direction) {
  row <- subset(deltas, candidate == name)
  round(if (direction == "profile") with(row, delta_profile) else with(row, delta_group_class))
}
profile_2 <- delta_of("profiles2_groups1_VVV", "profile")
profile_3 <- delta_of("profiles3_groups1_VVV", "profile")
group_2 <- delta_of("profiles2_groups2_VVV", "group")
group_3 <- delta_of("profiles2_groups3_VVV", "group")
group_4 <- delta_of("profiles2_groups4_VVV", "group")
stopifnot(profile_2 > 0, profile_3 < 0, group_2 > 0, group_3 > 0, group_4 > 0,
          group_2 > 10 * group_3)
```

For the `VVV` structure with one group class, a second profile lowers the BIC
by `r format(profile_2, big.mark = ",")` and a third raises it by
`r format(-profile_3, big.mark = ",")`, which appears in the table as a
negative decrease. With two profiles, a second group class lowers the BIC by
`r format(group_2, big.mark = ",")`, a third by `r group_3` and a fourth by
`r group_4`. The decreases are plotted for both directions, along the number
of profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the right.

```{r plot-deltas, fig.height = 5}
plot_selection(models, what = "deltas")
```

The knee summary scales both axes of a curve to the unit interval and finds
the candidate with the largest perpendicular distance below the straight
line from the first point to the last. This chord-distance rule is inspired
by Kneedle (Satopää et al., 2011), without its smoothing or sensitivity
thresholds. A nearly linear curve can have a very small maximum distance, so
the reported distance describes the strength of the bend as well as its
location. The knee is computed along the number of profiles for each number
of group classes, along the number of group classes for each number of
profiles, and across all candidates ordered by their number of parameters,
separately for each structure.

The lines of the `VVV` candidates:

```{r knees}
subset(get_results(models, "knees"), endsWith(line, "VVV"))
```

```{r knee-values, include = FALSE}
knees <- get_results(models, "knees")
group_line <- subset(knees, direction == "group_classes" &
                       line == "2 profiles, VVV")
knee_along_groups <- with(group_line, knee_candidate)
knee_stable <- with(group_line, stable)
group_knees <- with(subset(knees, direction == "group_classes" &
                             !is.na(knee_candidate)), knee_candidate)
stopifnot(knee_along_groups == "profiles2_groups2_VVV", isTRUE(knee_stable),
          all(grepl("_groups2_", group_knees)))
```

Along the number of group classes, the knee lies at two group classes for every number of profiles from two to four and every structure; with two profiles and `VVV`
it is `r knee_along_groups`, and it does not move when the largest candidate
is removed (`stable`). Along the number of profiles, the BIC of the `VVV`
candidates with two or more group classes does not fall beyond two
profiles, so those lines have no knee (`note`).

The heatmap displays each candidate's criterion value relative to the
minimum across the fitted grid:

```{r heatmap}
plot_selection(models, what = "heatmap")
```

## Classification quality

Every observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class.
Relative entropy summarizes these probabilities over all observations, from 0
when every observation is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1 when
every observation belongs to one class with certainty (Ramaswamy et al.,
1993). The average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean
posterior probability of that class among the observations assigned to it.
Higher AvePP values indicate greater posterior certainty within the assigned
class. The candidate table reports the lowest, highest and mean AvePP at each
level and the number of classes below a user-selected cutoff (`cutoff`,
default 0.8). This threshold is a descriptive screening choice, not a
validated criterion for selecting the number of classes.

```{r quality}
plot_selection(models, what = "diagnostics")
```

`get_results(models, "classification")` returns the AvePP of every class of
every candidate, with its size and the relative entropy of its level; for the
`VVV` candidates with two profiles:

```{r classification}
subset(get_results(models, "classification"), n_profiles == 2 & model == "VVV")
```

```{r quality-values, include = FALSE}
row_of <- function(name) subset(candidates, candidate == name)
group_entropy_of <- function(name) with(row_of(name), round(group_entropy, 3))
group_avepp_of <- function(name) with(row_of(name), round(group_avepp_min, 3))
entropy_2 <- group_entropy_of("profiles2_groups2_VVV")
entropy_3 <- group_entropy_of("profiles2_groups3_VVV")
entropy_4 <- group_entropy_of("profiles2_groups4_VVV")
avepp_2 <- group_avepp_of("profiles2_groups2_VVV")
avepp_4 <- group_avepp_of("profiles2_groups4_VVV")
profile_entropy_chosen <- with(row_of(chosen_name), round(profile_entropy, 3))
avepp_chosen <- with(row_of(chosen_name), round(avepp_min, 3))
stopifnot(entropy_2 > entropy_3, entropy_3 > entropy_4)
```

Separation of the students declines as group classes are added. With two
profiles and `VVV`, the group-level relative entropy is `r entropy_2` with
two group classes, `r entropy_3` with three and `r entropy_4` with four, and
the lowest group-class AvePP falls from `r avepp_2` to `r avepp_4`.

## Checks of the estimation

Replication of the selected likelihood across starts provides evidence of
numerical stability, but cannot establish that the global maximum has been
found. Boundary estimates and small profiles warrant investigation because
they can indicate a solution driven by limited support or a restrictive
parameter bound. Their interpretation depends on the fitted model and data.
Refitting with `boundary = "exclude"` selects among starts whose continuous
variance parameters are above their lower bounds. This option changes start
selection and does not by itself establish that the retained profiles are
substantively meaningful. The following plots summarize these diagnostics.

```{r trust}
plot_selection(models, what = "trust")
```

```{r smallest}
plot_selection(models, what = "smallest")
```

All of the plots for choosing the number of classes are produced together
with `plot_selection(models)`.

A candidate on a boundary whose smallest profile holds about one observation
is a degenerate solution, not a profile: a Gaussian profile centred on one
observation raises the likelihood without limit as its variances shrink, so
the reported likelihood is fixed by `min_variance`. The default,
`boundary = "allow"`, reports it, as Mplus does, with a warning.
`boundary = "exclude"` retains for each candidate the best start with no
variance at its lower bound, and is advisable when many starts are used,
since each additional start increases the chance of reaching such a
solution. Categorical indicators are unaffected.

```{r exclude, eval = FALSE}
excluded <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                              n_profiles = 1:4, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                              n_starts = 200, boundary = "exclude", seed = 1)
```

## Comparing candidates

Selected candidates are placed side by side with `compare_models()`.
Candidates are named as in the table or selected by a number of profiles or
group classes. The comparison adds the difference in BIC from the lowest of
the candidates compared and the BIC weight. The weight is
`exp(-delta_bic / 2)` normalized over the compared candidates (Wagenmakers &
Farrell, 2004). It summarizes relative support under this BIC approximation
and depends on the candidate set; it should not be interpreted as a
calibrated probability that a model is correct.

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

```{r compare-names}
compare_models(models, "profiles2_groups4_VVV", "profiles2_groups3_VVV",
               "profiles2_groups2_EEE")
```

The same comparison with labels, and with the candidate analysed below:

```{r compare-labels}
compare_models(models, bic = "profiles2_groups4_VVV",
               icl = "profiles2_groups3_VVV", awe = "profiles2_groups2_EEE",
               chosen = "profiles2_groups2_VVV")
```

The four structures with two profiles and two group classes, which shows
what the covariance structure adds:

```{r compare-select}
comparison <- compare_models(models, n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2)
comparison
plot(comparison)
```

The comparison keeps the fitted models. The AvePP of every class of every
compared model is returned by `get_results()`, and the model behind a row by
`get_candidate()`.

```{r compare-classification}
get_results(comparison, "classification")
```

## Testing neighbouring candidates

The bootstrap likelihood ratio test (McLachlan, 1987) compares two
candidates that differ by one class. Data sets are simulated from the
smaller candidate and both candidates are re-estimated on each. Of `B`
requested data sets, let `V` pass the estimation checks and `b` of those yield
a likelihood ratio at least as large as the observed one. The p-value is
`(b + 1) / (V + 1)` (Davison & Hinkley, 1997); the additional count includes
the observed statistic and precludes a p-value of zero. Invalid replicates
are reported, and the p-value is withheld when fewer than half the requested
replicates are valid. The test below compares two and three group classes
with two profiles and the `VVV` structure, the decision on which the criteria
disagree. Nineteen data sets keep the example brief; if all pass, the
smallest attainable p-value is 1/20 = 0.05. Applied analyses should use at
least 99 and inspect the valid count.

```{r blrt}
smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles2_groups2_VVV")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles2_groups3_VVV")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
plot(test)
```

```{r blrt-values, include = FALSE}
test_result <- get_results(test)
test_p <- with(test_result, p_value)
test_valid <- with(test_result, n_valid)
stopifnot(test_valid == 19, isTRUE(all.equal(test_p, 0.05)))
```

All `r test_valid` simulated data sets are valid, and none yields a
likelihood ratio as large as the observed one, so the p-value is
`r test_p`, the smallest attainable with this number of data sets. The result therefore favours three group classes over two, in agreement with
the BIC, at the smallest p-value that 19 bootstrap samples can give.

## The choice

The evidence points to two profiles with free within-profile covariances.
For the group classes, the bootstrap test and the BIC indicate that the data
contain structure beyond two group classes. The magnitude of that structure
is small: the second group class accounts for almost all of the improvement
in the BIC (`r format(group_2, big.mark = ",")` against
`r group_3` and `r group_4` for the third and fourth), the knee lies at two
group classes for every structure, and further group classes separate the
students less clearly. The analysis therefore continues with
`r chosen_name`, whose BIC is `r bic_gap` above the lowest. The small
improvements from further group classes have an identifiable source: a
student's engagement changes along the course sequence, a dependence between
the enrolments of a student that the multilevel model does not represent and
that additional group classes partly absorb. A latent transition model
represents it directly (see the
[latent transition analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lta.html)
article).

## Analysis of the chosen candidate

The candidate is taken from the fitted candidates by name with
`get_candidate()`. The numbers of classes with the structure give the same
model, as in `get_candidate(models, 2, 2, model = "VVV")`.

```{r chosen}
chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles2_groups2_VVV")
chosen
```

`chosen` is the same kind of object that `multilpa()` returns. Its summary
reports the estimates with their standard errors; `rows` limits the rows
printed from each table.

```{r chosen-summary}
print(summary(chosen), rows = 3)
```

The profiles are plotted as their means on the five indicators.

```{r chosen-profiles}
plot_profiles(chosen)
```

Each group class of students has its own distribution of the two profiles.

```{r chosen-prevalence}
plot_prevalence(chosen)
```

The classification diagnostics of the chosen model:

```{r chosen-diagnostics}
diagnostics(chosen)
```

The relative entropy of the chosen model is `r profile_entropy_chosen` for the
profiles and `r entropy_2` for the group classes; the lowest AvePP is
`r avepp_chosen` among the profiles and `r avepp_2` among the group classes.

```{r chosen-diagnostic-plots, fig.height = 7}
plot_diagnostics(chosen)
```

Each enrolment with its profile, its student's group class and its posterior
probabilities:

```{r chosen-assignments}
head(get_results(chosen, "assignments", data = course_engagement))
```

The profiles can also be related to an external variable. The following
analysis uses `three_step()` to estimate profile-specific means of
`previous_grade`, with the BCH correction for classification error (Bolck et
al., 2004; Bakk & Vermunt, 2016). The variable precedes the course enrolment,
so these comparisons describe associations rather than effects of profile
membership on grades.

```{r chosen-outcome}
three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
```

The previous grade averages 0.23 standard deviations above the mean before
enrolments of the first profile and 0.33 below it before enrolments of the
second, with 95% intervals that do not overlap.

## Other model types

### Latent class models

```{r lca-values, include = FALSE}
n_reports <- nrow(student_esm)
```

`student_esm` contains `r format(n_reports, big.mark = ",")` momentary
reports from students, with eight activities recorded as present or absent.
Declaring the indicators in `categorical` makes every candidate a latent
class model, and the candidates are named with `classes` in place of
`profiles`.

```{r lca}
activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
lca_models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:2,
                                categorical = activities, n_starts = 5,
                                seed = 1)
lca_models
plot_selection(lca_models, what = "diagnostics")
compare_models(lca_models, n_profiles = 3)
```

```{r lca-check, include = FALSE}
lca_row <- subset(as.data.frame(lca_models), candidate == "classes3_groups2")
lca_entropy <- with(lca_row, round(profile_entropy, 2))
lca_avepp <- with(lca_row, round(avepp_min, 2))
lca_lowest <- with(subset(get_results(compare_models(lca_models, n_profiles = 3),
                                     "comparison"), delta_bic == min(delta_bic)),
                   model)
stopifnot(lca_entropy < 0.6, lca_avepp < 0.7, lca_lowest == "classes3_groups2")
```

Among the three-class models, the model with two group classes has the
lower BIC. Its relative entropy is `r lca_entropy`, and its least distinct
class has an AvePP of `r lca_avepp`. This solution was reached by a single start and lies below the maximum found
with more starts in the [lca vignette](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lca.html)
(log likelihood -7,695.0 against -7,678.1), so its overlapping classes
reflect the search rather than the model; the
[two-level latent class analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lca.html)
vignette analyses these data with more starts.

### Single-level models

Observations without a grouping structure are modelled with
`enumerate_lpa()` for continuous indicators and `enumerate_lca()` for
categorical indicators. The candidates are named by their numbers of
profiles or classes alone. The example below enumerates the `srl` data under
the diagonal `VVI` structure, which shows how an unsuitable structure leads to
degenerate candidates; the
[latent profile analysis workflow](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/workflow-lpa.html)
analyses the same data with the full `EEE` structure.

```{r single}
srl_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                                   "self_efficacy", "self_regulation",
                                   "test_anxiety"),
                            n_profiles = 1:8, model = "VVI", n_starts = 10,
                            seed = 1)
srl_models
compare_models(srl_models, "profiles5", "profiles6", "profiles7")
plot_selection(srl_models, what = "deltas")
```

```{r single-check, include = FALSE}
srl_bic <- with(subset(get_results(srl_models, "best"),
                       criterion == "bic" & convention == "groups"),
                candidate)
on_boundary <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), boundary), candidate)
warned <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), nzchar(warnings)), candidate)
thin <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), grepl("membership mass for", warnings)),
             candidate)
seven_mass <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), candidate == "profiles7"),
                   round(min_gaussian_mass))
six_mass <- with(subset(as.data.frame(srl_models), candidate == "profiles6"),
                 round(min_gaussian_mass))
stopifnot(srl_bic == "profiles7",
          identical(on_boundary, c("profiles7", "profiles8")),
          identical(warned, c("profiles6", "profiles7", "profiles8")),
          identical(thin, warned), seven_mass <= 5, six_mass <= 12)
```

BIC is minimized by `r srl_bic`, but that candidate is a boundary fit: a
variance reached its lower bound, and one profile holds about `r seven_mass`
observations. Its low BIC reflects a nearly degenerate component, not a
better description of the data. The six-profile candidate is the best fit
that is not on the boundary, but it too has a profile of about `r six_mass`
observations, too few to determine its own ten means and variances. The
enumeration reports both with a `latents_thin_profiles` warning; such a
profile may be a spurious maximum, and the choice should be weighed against
the five-profile candidate, which `compare_models()` shows beside them. The
eight-profile candidate is also on the boundary, with two nearly empty
profiles, which marks the limit of what `r nrow(srl)` observations can
support. Every warning issued during the enumeration is retained in the
`warnings` column of the table.

### Missing values and scaled indicators

Two arguments alter the data to which the candidates are fitted and, like
`n_starts`, apply to all candidates. With `missing = "fiml"`, rows with some
indicators missing contribute through the indicators observed (full
information maximum likelihood); rows with every indicator missing are
excluded from the individual sample size, entropy and AvePP, since they
carry no information on class membership. `centering` subtracts and
`scaling` divides by a mean or standard deviation computed over the sample
(`"grand"`) or within each group (`"person"`); combined, they yield grand
or within-person z-scores. Information criteria are comparable only among
candidates fitted under the same settings. [Model
selection](model-selection.html) describes both with examples.

### Multiple covariance structures in single-level models

Specifying several structures in `model` multiplies the candidates, and the
structure is appended to each name. Because the numbers of classes then
match several candidates, a candidate must be specified by its full name.

```{r crossed}
crossed_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies",
                                       "intrinsic_value", "self_efficacy",
                                       "self_regulation", "test_anxiety"),
                                n_profiles = 2:4, model = c("VVI", "EEE"),
                                n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
crossed_models
compare_models(crossed_models, "profiles3_VVI", "profiles3_EEE")
```

### Latent transition models

With `time`, every candidate is a latent transition model over the
occasions, here the order of each student's enrolments in `sequence`. As in
the two-level grid above, the within-profile covariances are estimated
(`covariance_model = "full"`).

```{r transitions, warning = FALSE}
transition_models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                                       time = "sequence",
                                       covariance_model = "full",
                                       n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1,
                                       n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
transition_models
compare_models(transition_models)
```

```{r transitions-check, include = FALSE}
transition_table <- as.data.frame(transition_models)
stopifnot(all(with(transition_table, converged)),
          with(subset(transition_table, bic == min(bic)), candidate) ==
            "profiles2_groups1")
```

The BIC selects two profiles, the generating number, and every candidate
converges. The
[latent transition analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lta.html)
article enumerates profiles and group classes together.

```{r reference, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Call = c(
    "enumerate_classes(data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model)",
    "enumerate_classes(..., n_starts = , missing = \"fiml\", centering = , scaling = )",
    "enumerate_classes(..., boundary = \"exclude\")",
    "enumerate_classes(..., time = ), enumerate_lpa(), enumerate_lca()",
    "bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = , iter = )",
    "as.data.frame(models)",
    "get_results(models, \"best\")",
    "get_results(models, \"classification\")",
    "get_results(models, \"candidates\", cutoff = 0.9)",
    "get_results(models, \"deltas\", using = )",
    "get_results(models, \"knees\", using = )",
    "plot_enumeration(models), plot_enumeration(models, what = \"bic_groups\"), what = \"all\"",
    "plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = , model = )",
    "plot_enumeration(models, what = \"entropy\", \"avepp\" or \"diagnostics\", cutoff = )",
    "plot_selection(models, what = \"deltas\", \"heatmap\", \"smallest\" or \"trust\", using = )",
    "plot_selection(models)",
    "get_candidate(models, \"profiles2_groups2_VVV\"), get_candidate(models, 2, 2, model = \"VVV\")",
    "compare_models(models, \"name\", label = \"name\", ...)",
    "compare_models(models, n_profiles = , n_group_classes = )",
    "compare_models(name = fit, name = fit)",
    "get_candidate(comparison, \"name\")",
    "get_results(comparison, \"classification\")"),
  Result = c(
    "The fitted candidate models",
    "The same starts, missing-data handling, centring and scaling for every candidate",
    "Starts with a variance at its lower bound set aside for every candidate",
    "Transition models, single-level profile and class models",
    "Bootstrap likelihood ratio test of two neighbouring candidates",
    "One row per candidate with every column",
    "The candidate at the minimum of each criterion",
    "Size, AvePP and entropy of every class of every candidate",
    "The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff",
    "Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer",
    "Maximum chord-distance knee of each line, its range and its stability",
    "Information criteria across the candidates",
    "Division of profiles as more are added",
    "Entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates",
    "Decreases, distance from the lowest criterion, smallest class, estimation checks",
    "All of the plots for choosing the number of classes",
    "One fitted candidate",
    "Named candidates side by side",
    "All candidates with the given numbers of classes",
    "Fitted models side by side, on the same data",
    "The model behind a row of a comparison",
    "Every class of every compared model")),
  col.names = c("Call", "Result"))
```
